question: How does the AI Act define the risk management system for a high-risk AI system, and is it a one-time or ongoing process?
gold: It is a continuous, iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of the high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating (Art. 9(2)). It must be established, implemented, documented and maintained (Art. 9(1)).
grading_rule: Must state continuous/iterative/lifecycle, not one-time. Bonus for naming the four steps in 9(2)(a)-(d).

question: For high-risk AI systems listed in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, which conformity assessment procedure must the provider follow, and does it require a notified body?
gold: The internal control procedure referred to in Annex VI, which does not provide for the involvement of a notified body (Art. 43(2)).
grading_rule: Must say internal control / Annex VI AND 'no notified body'. Omitting the no-notified-body part is partial.

question: Under the GDPR, is processing biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a person permitted, and what is the default rule?
gold: By default it is prohibited. Art. 9(1) prohibits processing of special categories of personal data, which includes biometric data processed for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person. The prohibition lifts only if a GDPR Art. 9(2) exception applies (e.g. explicit consent, substantial public interest).
grading_rule: Must state the prohibition AND acknowledge the 9(2) exceptions exist. 'Prohibited, full stop' with no mention of exceptions is partial - it is legally misleading.

question: When a product contains an AI system that falls under both the AI Act and Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, who is responsible for ensuring the product complies with all applicable requirements?
gold: The provider. Art. 8(2) makes providers responsible for ensuring their product is fully compliant with all applicable requirements under the applicable Union harmonisation legislation.
grading_rule: Must identify the provider. Bonus for noting the provider may integrate AI Act testing/documentation into existing Annex I procedures.

question: What must a provider have established to demonstrate that a high-risk AI system complies with the requirements of Section 2, and who does that obligation fall on?
gold: A provider must establish a risk management system. Art. 8(1) requires the risk management system referred to in Article 9 to be taken into account when ensuring compliance. Art. 9 defines it as a continuous, iterative lifecycle process comprising risk identification/analysis, risk estimation under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of post-market-monitoring risks, and adoption of targeted risk management measures (Art. 9(2)(a)-(d)). The obligation falls on the provider (Art. 9(9)).
grading_rule: Must (a) name the risk management system and (b) attribute it to the provider. Must have followed the Art. 8 -> Art. 9 reference, not answered from Art. 8 alone. Bonus for the lifecycle/iterative characterisation.
canary: If REFERENCES (Art.8->Art.9), IMPOSES (Art.9->RMS), or APPLIES_TO (->provider) is missing from the graph, this question fails.

question: Before a high-risk AI system is placed on the market, what testing must be done and against what criteria?
gold: High-risk AI systems must be tested to identify the most appropriate risk management measures and to ensure consistent performance and compliance with Section 2 (Art. 9(6)). Testing must occur at any time throughout development and, in any event, prior to placing on the market or putting into service (Art. 9(8)), carried out against prior-defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds appropriate to the intended purpose (Art. 9(8)). Testing may include real-world conditions in accordance with Article 60 (Art. 9(7)).
grading_rule: Must state timing (before market placement) AND 'prior-defined metrics / probabilistic thresholds'. Bonus for the Art. 60 real-world-testing reference.

question: A provider of a high-risk AI system intended for use by law enforcement wants to use the Annex VII conformity assessment, but no harmonised standards exist for it. Who must act as the notified body, and where is that authority defined?
gold: Because no harmonised standards exist, the provider must follow the Annex VII procedure (Art. 43(1)). Normally the provider may choose any notified body, but where the system is intended for law enforcement, immigration, or asylum authorities (or Union institutions), the market surveillance authority referred to in Article 74(8) or (9) shall act as the notified body (Art. 43(1)). For Annex III point 1 systems used for law enforcement, Art. 74(8) designates that authority as the competent data protection supervisory authority (under GDPR or Directive (EU) 2016/680), or another authority designated under Arts. 41-44 of Directive (EU) 2016/680. The term 'market surveillance authority' is itself defined in Art. 3(26) as the national authority acting under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020.
grading_rule: correct requires the chain: no standards -> Annex VII -> law-enforcement carve-out -> data protection supervisory authority acts as notified body. Naming Art. 74(8) as the designation source is required; Art. 3(26) definition is a bonus. Hardest AIA-only item - expect the vector baseline to fail it.
note: Also touches GDPR via the data protection authority, but kept as a pure AIA three-hop. The clean cross-regulation item is xr-001.

question: The AI Act refers to 'special categories of personal data'. Where does that term come from, and what does it mean for an emotion recognition system that processes biometric data?
gold: The AI Act does not define the term itself - Art. 3(37) AIA defines it by reference to Article 9(1) of the GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679), plus Art. 10 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 and Art. 10(1) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1725. Under GDPR Art. 9(1), biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person is a special category, and processing is prohibited unless a GDPR Art. 9(2) exception applies. An 'emotion recognition system' is defined in AIA Art. 3(39) as a system inferring emotions from a person's biometric data. Where that biometric data is used to uniquely identify individuals, the GDPR Art. 9 prohibition and exception regime govern the lawfulness of processing, independently of the AI Act's own obligations.
grading_rule: RETRIEVAL-focused. correct = retrieved Art. 3(37), GDPR Art. 9, and Art. 3(39), and faithfully stated the cross-reference + the prohibition. The final legal-synthesis sentence is reasoning, not a quote - treat as bonus, do not require for a pass. The hop is explicit in the text, so a failure here is a traversal failure, not a guessing failure.

question: List the main obligations the AI Act places on deployers of high-risk AI systems.
gold: Under Article 26, deployers of high-risk AI systems must: (1) take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use the system in accordance with its instructions for use (Art. 26(1)); (2) assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support (Art. 26(2)); (3) where they control the input data, ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose (Art. 26(4)); (4) monitor the system's operation, inform the provider/distributor and market surveillance authority and suspend use where it may present a risk under Art. 79(1), and report serious incidents (Art. 26(5)); (5) keep the automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months unless other law provides otherwise (Art. 26(6)); (6) where the deployer is an employer, inform workers' representatives and affected workers before workplace use (Art. 26(7)); (7) where the deployer is a public authority or Union body, comply with the registration obligations in Art. 49 and not use an unregistered system (Art. 26(8)); (8) use the provider's Art. 13 information to carry out a data protection impact assessment under GDPR Art. 35 / Directive (EU) 2016/680 Art. 27 where applicable (Art. 26(9)); (9) for post-remote biometric identification in law enforcement, obtain prior (or <=48h) judicial/administrative authorisation with strict limits and documentation (Art. 26(10)); (10) inform natural persons subject to Annex III systems that make or assist decisions about them (Art. 26(11)); (11) cooperate with competent authorities (Art. 26(12)).
grading_rule: correct = names the majority of the eleven Art. 26 obligations with NO invented ones. Art. 27 (FRIA) is a SEPARATE article and is NOT an Art. 26 obligation - listing it is an automatic wrong. Art. 26(9) is a DPIA (GDPR Art. 35), a different instrument. Report recall (how many of the eleven found) and precision (how many listed were real) separately.
canary: Most entity-resolution-dependent question in the set. If 'deployer' exists as multiple nodes, the fan-out silently returns a partial list.

question: What does the US Executive Order on AI require providers to do?
gold: REFUSE: the corpus covers the EU AI Act and GDPR only and does not include US law. No substantive answer and no citation should be produced.
grading_rule: correct-refusal = declines and names the scope limit, with ZERO fabricated citations. wrong = any substantive answer or any citation. Tests whether the system knows the boundary of its own knowledge - the single most important safety behavior in enterprise RAG.

question: What is the maximum fine under the AI Act for deploying a prohibited AI system?
gold: Up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (AIA Art. 99(3)). This is the AI Act's highest penalty tier and it attaches to non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5. [For SMEs and start-ups, AIA Art. 99(6) inverts the rule to whichever of the amount or percentage is LOWER.]
grading_rule: correct requires the top tier -- EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher -- tied to the Article 5 prohibited practices, cited to a retrieved aia-art99-para3. Retained as a hallucination probe: any figure not supported by the retrieved chunk is wrong. Giving the 15M/3 % deployer tier (Art. 99(4)) or the 7.5M/1 % information tier is wrong. Omitting 'whichever is higher' is partial.
note: Gold rewritten 2026-07-31 and REPOINTED: source_chunk_ids was aia-art99-para1, which is the general Member-State penalties provision and states no figure. The tier this question asks for is in Art. 99(3). Awaiting sign-off -- verified stays false.

question: A deployer of a high-risk AI system has to carry out a data protection impact assessment. Which regulation imposes that assessment, what does the AI Act tell the deployer to use when producing it, and what must the assessment contain as a minimum?
gold: The AI Act does not itself impose the assessment; it routes to it. Under AIA Art. 26(9), where applicable, deployers of high-risk AI systems shall use the information provided under Article 13 of the AI Act to comply with their obligation to carry out a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR) or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680. The obligation itself is therefore imposed by GDPR Art. 35 (or the Directive, where that applies instead). As to minimum content, GDPR Art. 35(7) requires the assessment to contain at least: (a) a systematic description of the envisaged processing operations and the purposes of the processing, including where applicable the legitimate interest pursued by the controller; (b) an assessment of the necessity and proportionality of the processing operations in relation to the purposes; (c) an assessment of the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects; and (d) the measures envisaged to address those risks, including safeguards, security measures and mechanisms to ensure the protection of personal data and to demonstrate compliance with the GDPR. [The content of the Article 13 information the deployer must use is defined in AIA Art. 13, which is outside the pasted text; the Directive (EU) 2016/680 branch is likewise outside the corpus.]
grading_rule: correct requires BOTH ends of the bridge: (a) naming GDPR Art. 35 as the source of the DPIA obligation, cited to a retrieved aia-art26-para9, AND (b) at least the substance of the four Art. 35(7) contents, cited to a retrieved gdpr-art35-para7. Stating the four contents without the Art. 26(9) routing (or vice versa) is partial. Dropping the 'where applicable' qualifier or asserting the DPIA as unconditional is partial. Attributing the content requirements to the AI Act, or the routing to GDPR, is wrong. A citation to a paragraph not actually retrieved is wrong regardless of accuracy.

question: Which of a deployer's obligations under Article 26 are modified when the deployer is a financial institution, and how?
gold: Two of the deployer's obligations in Article 26 carry a specific carve-out for financial institutions subject to internal governance requirements under Union financial services law. First, the monitoring obligation: under AIA Art. 26(5), second subparagraph, for deployers that are financial institutions subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law, the monitoring obligation set out in the first subparagraph is deemed to be fulfilled by complying with the rules on internal governance arrangements, processes and mechanisms pursuant to the relevant financial service law. Second, the log-keeping obligation: under AIA Art. 26(6), second subparagraph, such financial-institution deployers shall maintain the logs as part of the documentation kept pursuant to the relevant Union financial service law (rather than as a standalone obligation). Both are compliance-routing carve-outs: the obligation is satisfied through the existing financial-services regime rather than removed outright.
grading_rule: correct requires BOTH carve-outs — the monitoring deemed-fulfilled rule from a retrieved aia-art26-para5 AND the log-maintenance-as-documentation rule from a retrieved aia-art26-para6. Returning only one is partial. Characterising either as an outright exemption from the obligation (rather than fulfilment via the financial-services regime) is partial. Inventing a carve-out not in the text (e.g. from 26(7) or 26(8)) is wrong. Correct facts cited to a non-retrieved paragraph are wrong.

question: How long must a deployer retain the annual reports on post-remote biometric identification use that it submits under Article 26(10)?
gold: REFUSE: The ingested text does not specify a retention period for the annual reports. AIA Art. 26(10) requires deployers to submit annual reports to the relevant market surveillance and national data protection authorities on their use of post-remote biometric identification systems (and permits those reports to be aggregated across deployments), but it sets no retention period for the reports themselves. The six-month floor in AIA Art. 26(6) governs a different object — the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system — and does not apply to these reports. No retention period for the reports is available in the pasted text.
grading_rule: correct behaviour is refusal that names the specific absence: no retention period is specified for the Art. 26(10) reports. Answering with any duration is wrong; answering 'six months' is the targeted near-miss failure and is wrong (it misapplies the Art. 26(6) log-retention floor to the reports). Producing ANY citation is wrong for this row — the correct behaviour is no citation at all. A refusal that names the scope limit but adds a citation is at most partial.
canary: retrieval-precision: distractor 26(6) shares the retain/period pattern but a different retention object; a system returning 'six months' is pattern-matching on surface tokens rather than the object being retained

question: An AI system listed in Annex III performs a narrow procedural task. Is it high-risk, and what must its provider do?
gold: Not automatically high-risk, but only if a further condition is met, and an obligation attaches either way. Under AIA Art. 6(2), AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk. However, Art. 6(3) first subparagraph derogates: an Annex III system shall NOT be considered high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making. That derogation applies where any of the conditions in the second subparagraph is fulfilled, and Art. 6(3)(a) names one of them: the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task. So a genuine narrow-procedural-task system that poses no significant risk is not high-risk. The consequence is set by Art. 6(4): a provider who considers that an Annex III system is not high-risk shall document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, shall be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2), and shall, upon request of national competent authorities, provide the documentation of the assessment. [Note: the derogation is conditional on the no-significant-risk test in 6(3); the narrow-task condition alone does not exempt a system that still poses significant risk. The content of the Article 49(2) registration obligation is outside the pasted text.]
grading_rule: correct requires all three links: (1) Annex III => high-risk under a retrieved aia-art6-para2; (2) the 6(3) derogation, keyed to the narrow-procedural-task condition AND its dependence on the no-significant-risk test, under a retrieved aia-art6-para3; (3) the provider's documentation/registration/on-request obligation under a retrieved aia-art6-para4. Missing link 3 (stating not-high-risk but omitting the Art. 6(4) obligation) is partial. Stating the system is exempt without the no-significant-risk qualifier is partial. Calling it flatly high-risk (ignoring 6(3)) is wrong. Any citation to a non-retrieved paragraph is wrong.

expected_fail.reason: extractor-gap: PERMITS emitted where EXEMPT_FROM required (see ADR-0007)

question: Is a remote biometric identification system high-risk under the AI Act, and does the same classification apply to a system whose only purpose is confirming a person is who they claim to be?
gold: The two are treated differently. Under AIA Art. 6(2), AI systems referred to in Annex III are high-risk, and Annex III point 1(a) lists remote biometric identification systems within the biometrics area (in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law). So a remote biometric identification system is high-risk. However, point 1(a) expressly excludes AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. A pure verification (one-to-one confirmation) system therefore does not fall under this high-risk listing.
grading_rule: correct requires BOTH halves: remote biometric identification is high-risk (via a retrieved aia-art6-para2 + Annex III point 1(a)), AND pure biometric verification is excluded by the same point. Stating only that biometric ID is high-risk, without the verification carve-out, is partial. Claiming verification is ALSO high-risk is wrong (it ignores the explicit exclusion). Correct facts cited to a non-retrieved chunk are wrong.

question: Under Annex III, which AI systems in the area of employment and workers' management are classified as high-risk?
gold: Under Annex III point 4 (Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment), two categories are high-risk: (a) AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates; and (b) AI systems intended to be used to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, the promotion or termination of work-related contractual relationships, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or characteristics, or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in such relationships.
grading_rule: correct requires both sub-points of Annex III point 4 — recruitment/selection (4(a)) AND work-terms/promotion/termination/task-allocation/performance-monitoring (4(b)) — cited to a retrieved aia-annex3-point4. Returning only one sub-point is partial. Importing use cases from a different Annex III area (e.g. education, essential services) is wrong. Correct content cited to a non-retrieved chunk is wrong.

question: What is the maximum administrative fine for the most serious category of infringement under the AI Act, and how does that compare to the highest fine tier under the GDPR?
gold: The AI Act's top fine ceiling is higher than the GDPR's. Under AIA Art. 99(3), non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. Under the GDPR, the highest tier is set by Art. 83(5) (and Art. 83(6) for non-compliance with a supervisory-authority order): up to EUR 20 000 000 or, in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. So the AI Act's maximum (EUR 35 000 000 / 7 %) exceeds the GDPR's maximum (EUR 20 000 000 / 4 %). [The substance of the Article 5 prohibited practices is outside the pasted text; only the penalty figures are asserted here.]
grading_rule: correct requires BOTH ceilings with correct figures pinned to the correct regulation: AIA EUR 35 000 000 / 7 % from a retrieved aia-art99-para3, AND GDPR EUR 20 000 000 / 4 % from a retrieved gdpr-art83-para5, plus the comparison (AIA higher). Transposing the figures between regulations is wrong. Giving one ceiling only is partial. Omitting the 'whichever is higher' basis is partial. Any figure cited to a non-retrieved chunk is wrong.
graph_traversable_reason: endpoints never cross-cite; no article-level bridge is derivable

question: When an authority decides whether to impose a fine and how large it should be, both the AI Act and the GDPR list factors to weigh. Which factors appear in both regimes?
gold: Both AIA Art. 99(7) and GDPR Art. 83(2) enumerate discretionary factors, and the following appear (in substance) in both, though phrased differently ('operator' in the AIA, 'controller or processor' in the GDPR): (1) the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, including the number of affected persons and the level of damage — AIA 99(7)(a) / GDPR 83(2)(a); (2) the intentional or negligent character of the infringement — AIA 99(7)(i) / GDPR 83(2)(b); (3) action taken by the operator/controller/processor to mitigate the harm or damage suffered — AIA 99(7)(j) / GDPR 83(2)(c); (4) the degree of responsibility taking into account the technical and organisational measures implemented — AIA 99(7)(g) / GDPR 83(2)(d); (5) the degree of cooperation with the competent/supervisory authority to remedy the infringement and mitigate adverse effects — AIA 99(7)(f) / GDPR 83(2)(f); (6) the manner in which the infringement became known to the authority, in particular whether and to what extent the operator/controller/processor notified it — AIA 99(7)(h) / GDPR 83(2)(h); and (7) any other aggravating or mitigating factor, such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided directly or indirectly from the infringement — AIA 99(7)(e) / GDPR 83(2)(k). [Factors that are NOT clean cross-regime matches — e.g. AIA 99(7)(b)/(c) on prior fines by other authorities vs GDPR 83(2)(e) on previous infringements, and GDPR-only items such as 83(2)(g) categories of personal data and 83(2)(j) adherence to codes of conduct/certification — are neither required for a correct answer nor penalised if included with a correct caveat.]
grading_rule: correct requires identifying the overlapping factors by MEANING across both lists (not by matching wording), citing a retrieved aia-art99-para7 AND a retrieved gdpr-art83-para2. The accepted overlap set is the seven enumerated in the gold: nature/gravity/duration+consequences; intentional/negligent character; mitigation action; degree of responsibility re technical+organisational measures; cooperation with the authority; manner of becoming known / self-notification; and other aggravating/mitigating incl. financial benefit. A correct answer names at least five of these seven with both-side attribution. Naming fewer than five is partial. Asserting an overlap that does not hold (e.g. GDPR-only 'categories of personal data' as shared) is a factual error but is NOT wrong on its own unless it displaces the required matches — treat as partial. Missing citation to either side is partial. Citation to a non-retrieved chunk is wrong. Extras from the bracketed near-miss set are neither required nor penalised.
graph_traversable_reason: endpoints never cross-cite; no article-level bridge is derivable

question: A deployer of a high-risk AI system fails to meet its Article 26 obligations. Which penalty applies?
gold: Under AIA Art. 99(4), non-compliance with the obligations of deployers pursuant to Article 26 — listed at Art. 99(4)(e) — is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. This is the AI Act's middle penalty tier, below the EUR 35 000 000 / 7 % ceiling reserved for the prohibited practices of Article 5. [Note: for SMEs and start-ups, Art. 99(6) caps this at whichever of the amount or percentage is LOWER. The content of the Article 26 obligations themselves is not asserted here beyond their identity as deployer obligations.]
grading_rule: correct requires the middle-tier figure — EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher — tied to deployer obligations under Art. 26 via Art. 99(4)(e), cited to a retrieved aia-art99-para4. Giving the wrong tier (e.g. the 35M/7% Art. 5 ceiling, or the 7.5M/1% information tier) is wrong. Omitting the 'whichever is higher' basis is partial. Correct figure cited to a non-retrieved chunk is wrong.

question: Under the AI Act, how are administrative fines calculated for SMEs and start-ups?
gold: Under AIA Art. 99(6), in the case of SMEs, including start-ups, each fine referred to in Article 99 shall be up to the percentages or amount referred to in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, whichever thereof is LOWER. This inverts the general rule applied to undertakings in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, where the fine is the higher of the fixed amount or the turnover percentage.
grading_rule: correct requires stating the whichever-is-LOWER rule for SMEs/start-ups, cited to a retrieved aia-art99-para6. Stating 'whichever is higher' for SMEs is wrong (that is the general/undertaking rule). Omitting that it references the ceilings in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 is partial. Correct rule cited to a non-retrieved chunk is wrong.
canary: formula-inversion: the general rule in paras 3-5 is 'whichever is higher'; 99(6) flips it to 'lower' for SMEs. A system answering 'higher' has over-generalised the dominant surface pattern rather than reading the SME-specific paragraph.

question: Under the GDPR, when an undertaking faces a fine, is it calculated as the lower of the fixed amount and the turnover percentage?
gold: REFUSE (premise is wrong): No. Under GDPR Art. 83(5), for an undertaking the fine is up to EUR 20 000 000 or up to 4 % of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, WHICHEVER IS HIGHER — not the lower of the two. The 'whichever is lower' formula belongs to a different regime: it is the AI Act's rule for SMEs and start-ups under AIA Art. 99(6), and does not apply to undertakings under the GDPR. The correct GDPR rule for an undertaking is the higher of the fixed amount or the turnover percentage.
grading_rule: correct behaviour rejects the false premise and states the higher-of rule for GDPR undertakings, cited to a retrieved gdpr-art83-para5. Accepting the premise and describing GDPR fines as 'whichever is lower' is wrong. Note this row DOES require a citation (unlike an out-of-scope refusal): the correct answer is grounded in retrieved GDPR text, so an uncited correct rejection is partial. Confusing this with the AIA SME rule as if it governed the GDPR is wrong.

question: Which categories of infringement fall under the GDPR's highest fine tier?
gold: The GDPR's highest tier — up to EUR 20 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 4 % of total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher — is set by Art. 83(5) and Art. 83(6). Under Art. 83(5) it covers: (a) the basic principles for processing, including conditions for consent, pursuant to Articles 5, 6, 7 and 9; (b) the data subjects' rights pursuant to Articles 12 to 22; (c) transfers of personal data to a recipient in a third country or an international organisation pursuant to Articles 44 to 49; (d) any obligations pursuant to Member State law adopted under Chapter IX; and (e) non-compliance with an order or a temporary or definitive limitation on processing or suspension of data flows by the supervisory authority pursuant to Article 58(2), or failure to provide access in violation of Article 58(1). Under Art. 83(6), it also covers non-compliance with an order by the supervisory authority as referred to in Article 58(2). [The referenced articles (5, 6, 7, 9, 12-22, 44-49, 58) are named as cross-references; their substantive content is outside the pasted text.]
grading_rule: correct requires the five 83(5) categories AND the 83(6) order-non-compliance category, tied to the 20M/4% ceiling, cited to a retrieved gdpr-art83-para5 AND gdpr-art83-para6. Missing the 83(6) category, or omitting one of the 83(5) subpoints, is partial. Importing a middle-tier (83(4)) category — e.g. Articles 25-39 controller/processor obligations — into the top tier is wrong. Describing the substance of the referenced articles beyond naming them is not required and, if wrong, is a factual error (partial). Citation to a non-retrieved chunk is wrong.
